text: Chapter 19, the distributed message queue. Let's see how it works in a few minutes.

A producer sends messages to a topic. The topic is split into partitions, spread across different brokers. Each message carries a partition key. Hash the key, take the remainder by the number of partitions, and that picks the partition. The same key always lands in the same partition, so ordering is only guaranteed within one partition.

Each partition is an append-only log. New messages go at the end and get an increasing offset. Topic, partition, and offset together locate any message. The log is cut into segments. Old segments are read-only, and only the newest one is writable. Retention is two weeks, and expired segments are deleted whole, never message by message.

Reading a message does not delete it. Each consumer group stores its own offset, to remember how far it has read. The orders group is at six, the analytics group is at nine, and they never interfere. To replay, just move the offset back. There is one log, but each group keeps its own position.

Within a consumer group, each partition is assigned to just one consumer at a time. That keeps the order inside the partition intact. Three partitions, three consumers, one each. A fourth consumer has nothing to do and sits idle. So active consumers never exceed the number of partitions. For more parallelism, add partitions.

When a consumer joins, leaves, or misses its heartbeat, a rebalance starts. Members talk to the group coordinator, which tells them in the heartbeat reply to rejoin. One member becomes the leader and computes the assignment. When B joins, it gets a partition. When B crashes, the partition goes back to A. During the handoff, old owners must stop first.

For fault tolerance, each partition has several replicas, and only one is the leader. Producers write to the leader, and followers pull from it. The committed offset is thirteen, and the leader has just written two more. Replicas two and three have caught up, so they are in the ISR, the in-sync replicas. Replica four lags too far, so it is removed. A message is committed once every replica in the ISR has it.

How many replicas must confirm a write is configurable. With ACK zero, the producer fires and forgets. It is fastest, but a lost message goes unnoticed. With ACK one, the leader confirms right away, but if it crashes before replicating, the message is lost. With ACK all, every in-sync replica must have it. It is slowest, but the most durable.

Delivery semantics depend on the order of processing and committing the offset. Commit first, then process, and a crash in between means the message is never processed. That is at-most-once. Process first, then commit, and a crash before the commit means it is read again after restart. That is at-least-once, and duplicates are possible.

At-most-once may lose messages. At-least-once never loses them, but may duplicate, so your business logic must be idempotent. Exactly-once is the friendliest for users, and the most expensive. Reordering the commit cannot achieve it. Writing to an external database also needs transactions or idempotency.
To recap Chapter 19. The partitioned log trades appending for throughput and ordering. Consumer groups track their own progress with offsets. Replicas and the ISR trade latency against durability.
